meta.blurb: Bathsheba Everdene turns down the shepherd who loves her, then inherits a farm and runs it alone. One careless joke, a valentine sent for fun, brings a rich farmer to her door. A soldier with a sword is waiting in the woods.
meta.bible: Gabriel Oak: a young sheep farmer, honest, patient, loyal; plays the flute; later Bathsheba's shepherd and bailiff. Bathsheba Everdene: a beautiful, proud, independent young woman who inherits her uncle's farm at Weatherbury. William Boldwood: a rich, serious, middle-aged farmer, about forty, a bachelor. Sergeant Frank Troy: a handsome, careless soldier. Fanny Robin: a young servant girl on Bathsheba's farm who loves Troy. Liddy Smallbury: Bathsheba's young maid and companion. Joseph Poorgrass: a shy, timid farm worker. Jan Coggan: a wise, good-humoured farm worker. Pennyways: the dishonest bailiff whom Bathsheba dismisses. Norcombe Hill: where Gabriel keeps sheep. Weatherbury: the village and Bathsheba's farm. Casterbridge: the market town; its hiring fair, corn market and workhouse. Bath: the city where Bathsheba and Troy marry in secret. Lulworth Cove: the bay on the Dorset coast where Troy swims. Dorset. California: where Gabriel thinks of going. Malthouse: the old building where workers drink and talk. Valentine. Christmas. Voice and tone: warm, wise and rural, with gentle humour; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore; Boldwood shoots Troy at his Christmas party and is sentenced to death, then reprieved; set in the English countryside of the 1800s.

B1B2: Gabriel Oak is a young sheep farmer who lives on Norcombe Hill. One morning he sees a wagon full of furniture go by, with a pretty girl sitting on top.
At the gate the girl has no money for the fee, so Gabriel quietly pays it for her. She does not thank him, and he is both amused and hurt.
Gabriel soon learns that the girl is Bathsheba Everdene, who lives with her aunt on a nearby farm. He visits them with a lamb as a gift, and he cannot stop thinking about her afterwards.
Gabriel asks Bathsheba to marry him, promising to love and protect her always. She kindly refuses, saying she wants a husband who can tame her, and she knows he never could.
Bathsheba leaves the district soon afterwards, and Gabriel returns sadly to his flock. He has two sheepdogs, an old one that knows its work and a young one that still has much to learn.
One night, while Gabriel sleeps, the young dog chases the whole flock to the edge of an old chalk pit. Every sheep goes over the edge, and in a single night Gabriel loses everything he owns.
Gabriel sells everything he owns to pay what he owes, and he is left with almost nothing. Yet he does not give way to despair, and he decides to look for work on another farm.
On a winter day Gabriel goes to the hiring fair at Casterbridge and stands among the other workers. Hour after hour passes, but nobody offers him a place.
On his way to Weatherbury, Gabriel sees a fire at a farm, and he runs to help. The men there are doing nothing useful, so he takes charge and saves the stores of hay.
When Gabriel asks the farm's owner for work, he is astonished to find that she is Bathsheba Everdene. She has inherited the farm from her uncle, and she gladly takes him on as her shepherd.

Bathsheba tells her workers that she will manage the farm herself, without any bailiff to help her. She sends away the dishonest Pennyways, who has been stealing from the farm, and the men begin to respect her.
Every evening the workers gather in the old Malthouse to drink and talk about their new mistress. Gabriel listens quietly, and he soon learns who is honest, who is lazy and who is shy.
One of Bathsheba's maids, Fanny Robin, has disappeared from the farm. Gabriel meets her on a dark road at night, gives her some money and promises to keep her secret.
Fanny was going to marry a soldier, Sergeant Troy, and she went to the church to meet him. But she had gone to the wrong church, and Troy was so ashamed and angry that he would not try again.
At the corn market in Casterbridge, every man turns to look at Bathsheba, except one. He is Farmer Boldwood, a rich, serious bachelor, and his coolness annoys her.
On Valentine's Day, Bathsheba and her maid Liddy are bored and playful, and they choose to send a card to Boldwood. Bathsheba seals it with red wax that says, “Marry me.”
Boldwood has never been in love, and the card disturbs his quiet life. He cannot stop looking at it, and soon he finds that he is thinking of Bathsheba day and night.
Boldwood goes to see Bathsheba and asks her seriously to be his wife. She is embarrassed and tells him that she does not love him, but she agrees to think about it.
Gabriel tells Bathsheba honestly that it was wrong to play with Boldwood's feelings. She is so angry at his words that she tells him to leave the farm at once.
Soon afterwards, Bathsheba's sheep find their way into a field of young clover and eat so much that they swell up. None of the men knows how to help them, and the sheep begin to die.
Gabriel arrives at once and, with a small sharp tool, cuts each sick sheep so that the gas can escape. The animals recover, and Bathsheba humbly asks him to stay on as her shepherd.
In early summer the men wash the sheep in a pool and then cut off their wool. Boldwood comes to watch the work, but his eyes are always on Bathsheba.
At the shearing supper, Boldwood quietly asks Bathsheba for her answer. She does not want to hurt him, so she says that she will give it to him later.

One night in a dark wood of fir trees, Bathsheba's dress catches on the spur of a soldier's boot. He is Sergeant Troy, the soldier Fanny loved, though Bathsheba does not know that, and his flattering words soon make her blush.
Troy takes her to a quiet hollow and shows her his skill with a sword. The blade flashes round her so closely that it cuts off a curl of her hair, and she is dazzled.
Gabriel has heard what kind of man Troy is, and he begs Bathsheba to keep away from him. She will not listen, and she tells Gabriel that he has no right to speak about her private life.
Boldwood meets Troy on the road and begs him to leave Bathsheba alone. Troy only laughs at him, and soon afterwards he leaves the village for the city of Bath.
Afraid of losing him, Bathsheba follows Troy to the city of Bath. There they are quietly married, and nobody in Weatherbury knows anything about it.
Bathsheba returns to the farm with her new husband, and the workers can hardly believe it. Boldwood hears the news with a face of stone, and something inside him begins to break.
Troy soon takes charge of the farm, but he has little interest in the hard work. He spends Bathsheba's money on drink and horse races, and she begins to worry.
At the harvest supper Troy gives the men so much drink that they fall asleep in the barn. Outside, black clouds are gathering, and only Gabriel sees the danger to the hay and the wheat.
Bathsheba hears Gabriel working in the dark, and she hurries out to help him. Together they cover the stacks in the lightning and rain, and by morning the harvest is safe.
Weak and ill, Fanny Robin drags herself along the road to Casterbridge, helped at last by a kind dog. She reaches the workhouse in the town, but she is too weak to recover, and she dies there.
The workhouse sends Fanny's coffin to Weatherbury, and Joseph Poorgrass is told to carry it. He stops at an inn on the way and arrives so late that the coffin must wait overnight at the farm.
Bathsheba cannot rest until she knows who is in the coffin, and she opens the lid. Inside lie Fanny Robin and a tiny baby, and she begins to guess who the father was.
Troy comes home and sees the coffin, and the colour leaves his face. He kisses Fanny, tells Bathsheba that this dead woman means more to him than she does, and walks out.
Troy spends a great deal of money on a stone for Fanny's grave and plants flowers there. Then heavy rain pours from the church roof and washes the flowers away, and he leaves the village in despair.
Troy goes to the Dorset coast, and one evening he swims in the sea at Lulworth Cove. A strong current carries him far from the land, and his clothes are left alone on the shore.
When the news reaches Bathsheba, she is stunned and sits in silence for hours. She puts on black clothes and begins to live quietly as a widow.
Gabriel begins to manage the whole farm, and the work goes well again. Bathsheba depends on him more each day, though he is careful never to speak of his feelings.
At last Boldwood begs her once more, and Bathsheba, tired and guilty, gives way. She promises to marry him after six years, if her husband has not returned by then.
On Christmas Eve Boldwood fills his house with light and guests, and he prepares a grand party. He hopes that Bathsheba will come and agree before everyone to be his wife.
Bathsheba goes to the party only because she is afraid of upsetting him. Boldwood begs her to promise once more, and he puts a ring into her hand.
Just then the door opens, and a tall man in a long coat steps into the room. It is Troy, who everyone thought was dead, and he tells Bathsheba to come home with him.
Boldwood, white with rage, takes a gun from the wall and fires at Troy. Troy falls to the floor and does not move again, and the room is filled with cries.
Boldwood walks through the night to Casterbridge and gives himself up at the prison. He has lost everything, and he does not try to run away.
At his trial the judge sentences Boldwood to death. Many people ask for mercy, saying that his mind has not been well for a long time, and the sentence is later changed to prison.
Bathsheba stays at home for weeks, pale and silent, and few people see her. Meanwhile Gabriel tells the village that he is going to leave and try his luck in California.
One evening she walks to his cottage and asks if it is true that he is leaving. When he says that gossip is hurting her name, she tells him that she would be glad to hear him ask her.
Gabriel and Bathsheba are married quietly at the village church, with only a few friends beside them. After so many years of patient love, he has at last won the woman who once said no.
C1C2: On a cold winter morning, Gabriel Oak, a sober young farmer who had lately taken a flock of his own on Norcombe Hill, watched a laden wagon creak along the road below. High among the tables and chairs sat a girl whose beauty startled him, though she seemed quite unaware of his gaze. When she took out a small mirror and studied her own face with obvious satisfaction, he smiled at her vanity and fell a little in love all the same.

At the toll gate the girl searched for a coin and found none, while the keeper waited with growing impatience. Gabriel stepped forward and paid the small sum himself, expecting at least a word of thanks for his trouble. She gave him none, and rode on with her chin lifted, leaving him to reflect that she was uncommonly proud for one so poor.

Gabriel soon discovered that the proud girl was Bathsheba Everdene, a lively, quick-tongued young woman who lived with her aunt at a farm beyond the hill. He called on them with a motherless lamb as a gift, and he found her even more charming by daylight than she had seemed from a distance. Before long he was thinking of her through every long hour of his work among the sheep, and he scarcely noticed the cold.

Gabriel, who had never been a man of many words, laid his plain offer before her: a small farm, a steady heart and a lifetime of devotion. Bathsheba thanked him gently, but declared that she did not love him and that she was far too independent to be any husband's property. What she wanted, she added with a laugh, was someone who could tame her, and she was quite certain that he never would.

Bathsheba left the district soon afterwards, and Gabriel went back to the long, lonely routine of the hill with a heavy heart. He tried to console himself with hard work, for his flock was growing and his name was beginning to be known among the farmers. Two sheepdogs kept him company, an old one that understood its duties perfectly and a young one that was eager, clumsy and untaught.

One night, while Gabriel slept in his hut, the young dog took it into its head to herd the flock, and drove it in a frenzy toward the edge of an old chalk pit. By the time Gabriel reached the place, the whole flock had gone over, and the hillside was silent. In a single night the work of years had been undone, and he stood there a ruined man.

Gabriel sold what little remained, paid his creditors in full, and found that he possessed hardly more than the clothes he stood in. It was a bitter fall for a man who had been so near to prosperity, yet he bore it without complaint. Setting his pride aside, he resolved to seek honest work on another man's land.

At the hiring fair in Casterbridge, Gabriel took his place among the shepherds, carters and ploughmen who waited for masters to choose them. The hours dragged by, the crowd thinned, and no farmer wanted a stranger whose fortune had gone into a chalk pit with his sheep. Dusk found him still unhired, cold and hungry, with nothing but his crook and his flute for company.

Walking by night toward Weatherbury, Gabriel saw a glow ahead and found a farm in flames, with a crowd of bewildered labourers watching a stack of hay burn. He seized a branch and a wet sack, ordered the men about with calm authority and stopped the fire before it could spread to the barn. When the danger was over, he stood blackened with smoke and so tired that he could hardly lift his arms.

When Gabriel asked the owner of the farm whether she needed a shepherd, he found himself face to face with Bathsheba Everdene, who had lately inherited the land from her uncle. She did not dwell on their old acquaintance, and he took care to say nothing of the past himself. Thus, on the very night he had lost all hope of work, the proud girl who had refused him became his mistress and employer.

Bathsheba called her labourers together in the yard and announced, with a boldness that startled them, that she would act as her own bailiff. She dismissed the dishonest Pennyways, who had been robbing the farm, and warned the others that she would watch every shilling. Some men grumbled that a woman could not manage a farm, but the shrewd ones noticed that she kept her word.

In the evenings the labourers gathered in the old Malthouse, where, over their ale, they discussed the strange new mistress and her ways. There was Jan Coggan, wise and good-humoured, and Joseph Poorgrass, who blushed at every remark addressed to him. Gabriel sat quietly among them, learning who was honest and who was idle, and winning their trust by saying very little.

A young servant named Fanny Robin vanished from the farm one evening, and Bathsheba was anxious and puzzled by her sudden departure. On a dark road that night, Gabriel met the girl by chance, pale and frightened, and she begged him not to reveal where she was going. Moved by pity, he gave her what money he could spare and promised to keep her secret.

Fanny Robin's secret was a soldier named Sergeant Troy, who had promised to marry her on a certain morning. She mistook the church and waited at the wrong door, while Troy, who had been waiting at the right one, felt himself made a fool of. Humiliated and furious, he refused to try again, and poor Fanny was left anxious and alone.

At the Casterbridge corn market, Bathsheba found that every man's eyes followed her, except those of a grave, handsome farmer who stood apart and did not so much as glance in her direction. This was William Boldwood, a wealthy and respected bachelor of about forty, whose calm was the talk of the district. Bathsheba, unaccustomed to being overlooked, felt her vanity prick her far more than she liked to admit.

On Valentine's Day, bored by a long winter afternoon, Bathsheba and her young maid Liddy decided to send a valentine to the one man in the district who ignored her. Bathsheba chose a seal of red wax stamped with the words “Marry me,” never imagining that her prank would be taken seriously. She addressed it to Farmer Boldwood and sent it off, laughing at her own daring.

To Boldwood, a solitary man whose life had passed in orderly calm, the little card with its red seal came as a thunderclap. He turned it over and over, wondering who could have written such words, and the mystery gradually warmed into an obsession. Before many days had passed, he had learned the sender's name, and all his quiet heart belonged to her.

A few days later Boldwood presented himself at her door, grave and trembling, and asked her plainly to become his wife. Bathsheba was embarrassed to find that her joke had been taken so seriously, and she told him honestly that she did not love him. He begged her only not to decide in haste, and she, softened by his sincerity, agreed to consider the matter.

Gabriel, who could not bear to see a good man trifled with, told Bathsheba plainly that her valentine had been a cruel and thoughtless joke. Her face flamed with anger, for nobody had ever spoken to her so frankly, and least of all a man she had once refused. In a rage she ordered him to leave the farm at once, and he calmly gathered his belongings and went.

Soon afterwards the flock found its way into a field of fresh clover and gorged itself until the animals swelled with gas and began to collapse. The labourers stood about in helpless confusion, for none of them knew the cure, and the best of Bathsheba's sheep lay dying before her eyes. At last a boy was sent running to find Gabriel Oak, the one man who could save them.

Gabriel came without a word of reproach and went down on his knees among the suffering animals, making a swift incision in each swollen side with his thin, hollow instrument. One by one the sheep recovered, the dreadful swelling subsided, and the farm's finest ewes were saved from certain death. Bathsheba, her pride gone for once, asked him to remain, and he agreed, though he would never again presume to flatter her.

In early summer the men washed the flock in the river pool and carried the clean animals to the great barn for shearing, where Gabriel worked beside the others with calm skill. Boldwood, who had no work to do there, came and stood at the edge of the barn, unable to take his eyes from Bathsheba. She pretended not to notice him, though she felt the weight of his gaze like a hand on her shoulder.

At the shearing supper, with the whole farm singing and laughing around them, Boldwood drew Bathsheba aside and asked in a trembling voice whether she had made up her mind. She did not wish to wound him, yet she could not bring herself to give her promise, and so she said only that he would have his answer in time. He went home that night happier than he had been in years, taking her uncertainty for hope.

One dark evening, Bathsheba was walking home through a wood of fir trees when the spur of a soldier's boot caught in the hem of her dress. The soldier was Sergeant Troy, a handsome, careless young man, and he apologised with so much charm and so many compliments that she was left blushing in the darkness. She did not know that he was the same man whom poor Fanny Robin loved and had waited for.

In a green hollow, away from every watching eye, Troy showed Bathsheba the sword exercise that he had learned in the army. The blade flashed and whirled around her in a bright net of light, so close that it sliced off a single lock of her hair without touching her skin. When it was over she stood breathless and dazzled, and she knew that she had never felt anything like it.

Gabriel, who had heard enough of Troy's reputation to be uneasy, begged Bathsheba to be careful of a man whose charm was so much greater than his character. She answered with cold fury that her private affairs were none of his business and that he should mind his sheep. He bowed his head and said nothing more, though his love for her was as strong as ever and his anxiety grew with every day.

Boldwood stopped Troy on the road and begged him to keep away from Bathsheba, but the young soldier only laughed at his earnestness. Troy declared that no man alive could tell him where to go or whom to speak to, and he walked on whistling into the dusk. Soon afterwards he left Weatherbury for the city of Bath, and Boldwood was left alone with his dread.

Fearing that she might lose him, Bathsheba followed Troy to the city of Bath, ignoring every sensible warning that she had been given. There, in a few hurried days, the proud young farmer who had boasted that no man would tame her gave herself to a soldier she scarcely knew. They were married quietly and in secret, and nobody in Weatherbury suspected a thing.

Bathsheba came home to Weatherbury as Mrs Troy, and the news ran through the village faster than any rumour had ever done. Her workers were astonished, Gabriel bowed his head in private grief, and Boldwood, who had trusted her promise of an answer, was struck as though by a blow. The gentle patience of the man who had waited so long turned slowly into something darker and far more dangerous.

Troy took charge of the farm with grand gestures and little patience, for he had no taste for the steady labour that it required. He gambled on the horse races, laid bets he could not afford, and spent his wife's money as though it flowed from a spring that never ran dry. Bathsheba watched in growing alarm as the confident, independent woman she had been began to slip away.

On the night of the harvest supper, Troy kept the labourers' cups full until the barn rang with song and then fell silent in drunken sleep. Outside, heavy clouds were piling up in the sky, and Gabriel, who could read the weather as other men read print, saw that the ripened crops stood in terrible danger. He alone was sober enough to act, and he turned his steps toward the stacks.

Bathsheba, finding her husband insensible, hurried out into the dark to help Gabriel, who was already working on the stacks by the glare of the lightning. All through the night she handed up the sheaves and ropes while he spread his coverings against the lashing rain, and neither of them spoke a word that was not needed. By morning the harvest was safe, and in the grey light she looked at him with a new and humbled gratitude.

Fanny Robin, weak with illness and hunger, dragged herself along the road toward Casterbridge, resting at every milestone, until a stray dog came to her aid and let her lean upon it. She reached the workhouse at last, but the long journey had broken her, and she died there soon afterwards. No one in Weatherbury knew where she had gone, and the truth was destined to reach them in a terrible way.

The coffin was sent to Weatherbury on a cart driven by Joseph Poorgrass, who, being timid and easily persuaded, lingered so long at an inn along the way that the hour grew very late. When he at last reached the village, Gabriel judged that no one should see the coffin in the dark, and he had it taken to Bathsheba's house to wait until morning. The neighbours, meanwhile, were already whispering behind their hands about who might lie inside, and Gabriel could do nothing to stop it.

Bathsheba, tormented by the whispers she had heard and unable to rest, lifted the lid of the coffin herself. Inside lay Fanny Robin and a tiny baby, so still and pale that grief and shock struck her at once. A dreadful suspicion, long refused, rose in her mind, and she understood who the father of that child must be.

When Troy entered the room and saw what lay there, his careless confidence broke into pieces, and he stood stricken for a long moment. He bent and kissed the dead girl, and then, with a cruelty that Bathsheba never forgot, he told his wife that Fanny, dead as she was, meant more to him than she had ever done. He walked out of the house, and she was left alone with her sorrow and her shame.

Troy ordered an expensive headstone for Fanny's grave and planted the earth with flowers, as though lilies could undo what neglect had done. Yet a torrent of rain poured from a gargoyle on the church roof and washed the flower beds into ruin. Seeing the work of his remorse destroyed, he turned away from the churchyard and, soon afterwards, from Weatherbury altogether.

Troy wandered to the Dorset coast, and one evening he went swimming in the sea at Lulworth Cove, leaving his clothes upon the shore. A strong current seized him and carried him far from the land, and when darkness fell, there was no sign of him in the water. Those who found his belongings had no doubt that the sea had taken him, and they carried the news to Weatherbury.

The news struck Bathsheba like a blow, and for days she sat withdrawn and silent, tormented by the memory of her mistakes. She put on black clothes and took no part in village life, thinking herself unworthy of any happiness. The proud mistress of Weatherbury had been humbled, and she now moved about her house like a shadow.

Gabriel took over the management of the farm, and under his steady hand the fields prospered and the accounts grew healthy again. Bathsheba came to rely on his judgment in everything, though he took care never to presume upon her trust or to speak of what he felt. Meanwhile Boldwood watched from his own land, patient and silent, as a man waits for the ice on a pond to melt.

Boldwood returned to her again and again, until Bathsheba, weary, guilty and unable to bear his suffering, gave way at last. She promised that if her husband had not been seen by then, she would marry Boldwood after six years, when the law would count Troy as dead. It was a promise made out of pity rather than love, and she regretted it almost as soon as the words had left her lips.

On Christmas Eve, Boldwood, who seldom entertained, filled his great house with candles, holly and music, and set out a splendid supper. Everything was arranged for one purpose, which was that Bathsheba should come and be seen as the woman who would one day be his wife. He waited in the glittering rooms, hopeful and anxious, like a man who has staked all his life on a single throw.

Bathsheba went to the party with reluctance, driven by her guilt and by the fear of what disappointment might do to him. In a quiet corner, Boldwood begged her to repeat her promise, and he pressed a ring into her hand as proof of his faith. She trembled and answered him as gently as she could, though every nerve in her body longed to be out of the house.

At that moment the door swung open, and a tall figure in a heavy coat stood upon the threshold, scanning the faces before him with an easy, mocking smile. It was Troy, whom the whole district believed to be lying at the bottom of the sea, and the sight of him drained the blood from every face. Taking no notice of the guests, he took Bathsheba by the arm and ordered her to come away with him.

Boldwood, who had stood like a man turned to stone, suddenly crossed the room, took a loaded gun from the wall and fired at Troy without a word. The soldier fell to the floor, and a silence more terrible than any scream gripped the room before the cries and the weeping began. Troy lay dead in the middle of the festive hall, and the Christmas lights shone down on him as brightly as ever.

Boldwood walked through the cold night to Casterbridge, where he handed himself over to the keepers of the county jail and made no attempt to deny what he had done. All the rage had left him, and in its place was a dull, hopeless calm, as though the man he had once been had died along with Troy. Behind him, in Weatherbury, Bathsheba was carried home half unconscious, and Gabriel took charge of everything.

At the trial the judge pronounced the sentence of death, which the law required. Yet the people of Weatherbury petitioned for mercy, pointing out that Boldwood's behaviour had grown steadily stranger ever since the day the valentine arrived. Their appeal was heard, and the sentence was changed to imprisonment, so that his life was spared though his freedom was gone for good.

For weeks Bathsheba shut herself away, pale and silent, and she scarcely looked at the farm that had once been her pride. Gabriel, who had borne her moods and her troubles for so long, concluded that there was no longer a place for him, and let it be known that he would soon leave for California. When the news reached her, a sorrow she had not expected settled on her heart.

One evening she walked to his cottage and asked, with a stiff pride that did not quite conceal her distress, whether it was true that he meant to go away. Gabriel replied that gossip about them was harming her good name, and that he could not in honour remain unless he might be her husband. Bathsheba, after a long pause, made him understand that she would be glad if he asked her, and that she had never known a truer friend.

In the end they were married very quietly at the village church, with a few friends beside them and none of the show that Bathsheba had once admired. The proud girl who had wanted to be tamed by nobody had learned the worth of a steady heart, and Gabriel, who had loved her through ruin, fire, storm and sorrow, felt his long patience rewarded. That night the friends gathered at the house and sang beneath the windows, and the song carried far across the quiet fields.
